drills.q: What percentage of traffic does a canary deployment typically start at, and does its output reach real users?
drills.a: Typically 1-5% to start, ramping to 20%/50%/100%. Yes -- unlike shadow, canary output DOES reach real users at whatever percentage is currently routed to it.

drills.q: True or false: reverting the serving container to the previous model version is a complete rollback.
drills.a: False -- a complete rollback also needs to address the response/feature cache, the feature pipeline's schema compatibility, and any batch/offline scoring jobs still running the bad version.

drills.q: What does CML (Continuous Machine Learning) add to a generic CI runner?
drills.a: It posts model metric comparisons and plots directly as pull-request comments and can provision cloud GPU runners for training -- making a model-quality regression visible in code review like a failing test.

drills.q: Explain why shadow deployment gives a statistical advantage over an unpaired A/B comparison, in terms of variance.
drills.a: Shadow sends the identical request to both models, producing paired observations -- shared request-level noise cancels out in the paired difference, reducing the variance of the estimated effect compared to an unpaired comparison across two separate traffic groups that don't share the same requests.

drills.q: A CI gate passes a new model because it clears an absolute AUC threshold of 0.85. What's the flaw in this gate design?
drills.a: It doesn't compare against the CURRENT CHAMPION's metric on the same fixed eval set -- if the champion is at 0.90 AUC, a 0.85 model is a real regression that an absolute-threshold-only gate would let through.

drills.q: Design a rollback for a real-time recommendation model with a response cache and a nightly batch re-scoring job. What does a naive rollback miss?
drills.a: A naive rollback only reverts the serving container. The full rollback needs: cache entries invalidated or version-tagged so stale bad-version outputs stop serving, the feature pipeline confirmed compatible with the reverted version's expected schema, and the nightly batch job's model version explicitly updated since it runs on a separate schedule and won't pick up a serving-only rollback.

drills.q: Explain how a rollback can itself introduce training-serving skew.
drills.a: If the feature pipeline was updated to support the newer model version (e.g. added a feature) and isn't reverted alongside the model, the rolled-back-to older model now receives feature vectors in a shape/distribution it was never trained on -- a mismatch the rollback created, not one that pre-existed.

drills.q: Why can shadow deployment never validate whether a new model improves a real business outcome, no matter the traffic volume?
drills.a: The shadow model's predictions are logged but never returned to a user or acted upon -- the causal path from 'model outputs X' to 'a real decision or action changes as a result' is never exercised, so you can measure that predictions differ but never that the difference is good.

drills.q: Design a canary ramp gate that decides 'hold / ramp / rollback' automatically rather than relying on a human glancing at a dashboard. What does it need before it can make any decision?
drills.a: It needs a pre-registered minimum sample size (based on a chosen minimum detectable effect) and a significance threshold (e.g. alpha=0.05) defined BEFORE the canary starts. The gate holds until sample size is reached, runs a significance test (e.g. t-test) on the outcome metric, ramps if canary is significantly better, rolls back if significantly worse, and holds if not yet significant.

drills.q: Why is shadow deployment fundamentally unable to validate a contextual bandit system, unlike a standard classifier?
drills.a: A bandit's future inputs depend on its own past served actions (the exploration/exploitation history) -- a shadow-mode bandit's logged predictions reflect what it WOULD have shown, but never generates the real served-action history that drives what the bandit would actually see and learn from next, so the comparison is measuring a structurally different process than real deployment.

drills.q: A fraud-detection canary shows improved fraud catch-rate at 20% traffic. Is that sufficient to ramp to 50%? What else must be checked?
drills.a: No -- false-positive rate must also be checked and gated, not just catch-rate/recall. A model that catches more fraud while also blocking significantly more legitimate transactions is a real regression on user experience and revenue even though the primary metric improved; both metrics need significance checks before ramping.
